metadata.title: The Target That Moved
metadata.voice_policy: week-2 spec specifies af_kore; week 1 used am_onyx. Flagged as a documented re-voice.
metadata.note: STEM/AI explainer built on Kehinde's own DQN LunarLander repo. The ONE idea: a DQN computes its target with the same network it is updating, so the target moves every time it learns. Freeze a copy and the target holds still. Every figure is measured in his repo. All components have registered 916 variants.

props.command: My trained DQN for LunarLander scores -391 over 100 greedy episodes. A uniformly random policy scores -213 on the same environment, so my trained model is worse than random. Help me find the cause rather than just training it longer.

beats.new_visual_element: Hesitant writer, the overview corrected on screen
beats.narration: I assumed it needed more training. It did not. It was chasing a target that moved every single time it learned anything, and you cannot hit a target that runs away from you.

beats.narration: First, the measurement, because this is the part people skip. I ran the saved model over a hundred fresh episodes with exploration turned off. Mean reward, minus 391. Then I ran a policy that just picks a thruster at random. Minus 213. My trained network was nearly twice as bad as guessing.

beats.narration: Here is what was actually wrong. The network learns by comparing its guess to a target, and that target is built from the network's own opinion about the next move. But it was using the very same weights it was busy updating. So every step that improved the guess also shifted the target it was being measured against.

show.event: The question sets: 'Which network computes the target?'
Left branch fills: A FROZEN COPY, held still while you learn
Right branch fills terracotta: THE SAME ONE, the target moves as you learn
Resolver lands: FREEZE A COPY

branches.label: THE SAME ONE
branches.fix: The target moves as you chase it.

resolver.label: FREEZE A COPY
resolver.detail: Sync it from the live network every 10 episodes.

beats.narration: The fix is small enough to fit on one screen. Keep a second frozen copy of the network, sync it from the live one every ten episodes, and compute the target from the frozen copy instead. Nothing else changed. Not the update rule, not the replay buffer, not the rewards.

shot.media_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW: the real change from the repo, trimmed to the lines that teach.

show.event: Code card opens, titled DQNlunar.py
The broken line reveals: target from the live network
The fixed lines reveal: a frozen target network, synced every 10 episodes
Spark line holds: the target has to hold still

props.title: DQNlunar.py
props.code:
# before: the target uses the network being updated
target = reward + gamma * policy_net(next_state).max()

# after: a frozen copy computes the target
target_net = copy.deepcopy(policy_net)
target_net.eval()

target = reward + gamma * target_net(next_state).max()

# resynced from the live network every 10 episodes
if episode % 10 == 0:
    target_net.load_state_dict(policy_net.state_dict())
props.sparkLine: The target has to hold still.

beats.narration: Then I retrained and measured the same way. Mean reward went from minus 391 to minus 13.9. And the number I care about more: episodes that actually landed went from zero out of a hundred to fifty-two out of a hundred. Not solved by the textbook standard, but it lands about half the time now instead of never.

beats.narration: So the lesson I would keep. Measure against a dumb baseline before you tune anything, because random is a real opponent and mine was beating me. A learning curve that gets more volatile over time is diverging, not warming up. And when something is not learning, look for what is moving that should be still.

show.event: Artifact card opens, titled 'What the bug taught me'
Five numbered lines stagger in
The last line holds longest

artifactLines: Always measure against a random baseline first.
Mine scored -391. Random scored -213. Random won.
Rising volatility is divergence, not slow learning.
When learning stalls, find what is moving that should be still.
Report what you measured, not what rounds up nicely.

beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the viewer's prompt typed
beats.narration: Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take any model you have trained, and before you tune it further, build the dumbest baseline you can: random guessing, or always predicting the most common answer. Score both the same way on the same held-out data. Tell me the two numbers side by side. If your model does not clearly beat the dumb one, the problem is not the hyperparameters. Run that before your next training job, because it is the cheapest experiment you will ever do.

If the model does not clearly beat the baseline, tell me what to investigate instead of which hyperparameters to change.
